summary: Finding where to test equipment and procedures on Earth is an early challenge for teams preparing to explore the Moon and Mars. AZZU Atlas is an interactive map that helps teams decide which terrestrial sites to evaluate first. It compares the terrain of candidate sites with selected lunar and Martian regions and shows where their slopes and elevation ranges are similar. In one prototype run, 804 of 204,239 Earth tiles that passed a vegetation screen met the terrain criteria for the base of Mount Sharp on Mars. The atlas turns a broad search into a shortlist for field evaluation.
details:
AZZU Atlas helps exploration teams shortlist terrestrial sites for testing equipment, instruments, and field procedures. A user can explore candidate sites on a map and compare their terrain with a selected lunar or Martian reference. The atlas shows the differences behind each comparison so teams can see why a site is worth a closer look.

The prototype compares three terrain measures across areas of the same size: median slope, the 90th-percentile slope, and the difference between the 95th and 5th elevation percentiles. The candidate catalog also applies a vegetation screen using NASA MODIS data. In one run for the base of Mount Sharp on Mars, 804 of 204,239 previously screened Earth tiles met the terrain criteria.

We combined geospatial analysis, software development, and design. Python processes the elevation data, PostgreSQL with PostGIS stores and ranks the results, and FastAPI serves the map and comparisons. The React landing page introduces the problem through the Moon, Mars, and their terrestrial analogs. Our next step is to evaluate shortlisted sites in the field and determine which are suitable for specific tests.
